prompt.context: Our client is the CEO of an Australia-based winemaker that is the market leader in its country. The company has two types of products: bottled wine and boxed wine. Recently, profits have been decreasing, and the CEO believes that this is due to losses in the boxed wine division.
prompt.question: We need to assess the situation and provide a recommendation. Specifically: (1) What factors should we consider to determine whether the boxed wine is a good business? (2) What is the profitability of each of the two divisions? (3) What is our recommendation?

clarifying_info.q: Is the company currently profitable overall?
clarifying_info.a: No, the company is currently losing money.

clarifying_info.q: How are sales split between bottled and boxed wine?
clarifying_info.a: Sales are split evenly between the two divisions.

clarifying_info.q: What is the price per unit for each product?
clarifying_info.a: Bottled wine sells for AUS$5 per unit; boxed wine sells for AUS$10 per unit.

clarifying_info.q: How much wine is in each unit?
clarifying_info.a: Bottled wine contains 750ml; boxed wine contains 3 liters. A plastic bag holds the wine inside the box.
Both products have an overhead of AUS$0.50 per unit.

clarifying_info.q: What are the raw material (grape) costs?
clarifying_info.a: Raw material (grapes) costs AUS$2 for bottled wine.

clarifying_info.q: What are the packaging and other variable costs?
clarifying_info.a: Packaging costs AUS$1 for both products. Other variable costs (distribution and labor) are AUS$1 per bottle and AUS$2 per box.

clarifying_info.q: Are the same grapes used for both products?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — and that is a key issue to explore.

framework: Understand revenue structure: price per unit, volume split, total revenue by division
Map all costs per unit: raw materials (grapes), packaging, other variables (distribution and labor), and overhead
Calculate unit-level contribution margin and profit for each division
Identify the root cause of losses in the boxed wine division
Assess whether the cost structure is appropriate given the price and customer segment
Develop a recommendation to restore profitability

questions.prompt: Calculate the raw material (grape) cost for the boxed wine unit.
questions.guidance: Because the box contains 3 liters versus 750ml in a bottle, the volume ratio is 4:1. If grapes cost AUS$2 for a bottle, they should cost AUS$8 for a box (same quality grapes, 4x the volume).

math.setup: Volume ratio = 3,000ml / 750ml = 4. Grape cost for box = AUS$2 × 4.
steps: AUS$2 × 4 = AUS$8 grape cost per box

questions.prompt: Calculate the unit profitability of bottled wine.
questions.guidance: Sum all per-unit costs: raw materials + packaging + other variables + overhead, then subtract from price.

questions.prompt: Calculate the unit profitability of boxed wine.
questions.guidance: Apply the same cost structure with the 4× grape cost derived in the previous step.

steps: Profit: AUS$10.00 − AUS$11.50 = −AUS$1.50 ... note casebook states −AUS$0.50; reconcile: overhead AUS$0.50, grapes AUS$8, packaging AUS$1, other AUS$2 → total AUS$11.50 vs price AUS$10 → loss AUS$1.50. Casebook summary states −AUS$0.50 (may omit overhead from their quick summary). Core insight: boxed wine is unprofitable.
math.answer: Loss per box (per casebook): AUS$0.50 loss; full cost build gives AUS$1.50 loss if overhead included

questions.prompt: Why is the cost-to-price ratio so unfavorable for boxed wine compared to bottled wine?
questions.guidance: The volume ratio is 1:4 (bottle to box) but the price ratio is only 1:2 (AUS$5 vs AUS$10). Using the same quality grapes for both products means grape cost scales 4× while revenue scales only 2×. Boxed wine likely serves a lower-end or bulk business customer who is price-sensitive, which justifies a lower-quality (cheaper) grape.

brainstorming.prompt: What areas of discussion should you explore to fully assess whether the boxed wine division is a good business?

categories.name: Revenue
ideas: Price per unit for each product
Who the customers are and what they are willing to pay

categories.name: Costs
ideas: Raw material (grape) cost and quality level

categories.name: Customer & Market
ideas: Target customer for bottled wine vs. boxed wine (premium vs. bulk/business)
Price sensitivity of boxed wine buyers
Market growth trends for each segment

categories.name: Operations
ideas: Whether the same grapes must be used for both products

recommendation: The boxed wine division is currently unprofitable because grape costs (which scale 4× relative to bottle) far exceed the revenue premium of the box format (which scales only 2×).

The company should source lower-cost grapes specifically for the boxed wine product line. Because boxed wine caters to bulk/business buyers rather than premium consumers, using the same high-quality (and high-cost) grapes as the bottled line is not justified by the price point.
Even a modest reduction in grape cost per box would restore profitability in the division.
risks: Lower-quality grapes could damage brand perception if the link between bottled and boxed products is strong in the market.
Existing supplier contracts may limit the ability to switch quickly or cheaply.
Competitors may already be sourcing cheaper grapes, limiting pricing power further.
next_steps: Identify alternative grape suppliers or lower-tier grape sources suitable for the boxed wine segment.
Conduct a brand perception analysis to assess risk of quality dilution.
Model the break-even grape cost reduction needed to make the boxed division profitable.
Evaluate whether the price of boxed wine can be increased given market conditions.
